nameStory: Hazel dodder gets its name from its preference for wrapping around hazel bushes and other shrubs. The word 'dodder' comes from an old Germanic word meaning 'to shake' or 'tremble,' referring to how these parasitic vines seem to quiver and move as they search for host plants to attach to.
description: Hazel dodder is a fascinating parasitic vine that looks more like orange spaghetti than a typical plant. Instead of leaves, it has thin, twisting orange or yellow stems that coil around host plants like hazel, elderberry, and other shrubs. This unusual plant has given up making its own food through photosynthesis and instead steals nutrients directly from other plants through specialized root-like attachments. The vine can spread several feet, creating tangled orange masses that are quite striking against green foliage.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Thin, thread-like orange to yellow stems that twist and coil around host plants, completely lacking normal green leaves

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white or cream-colored flowers clustered in small, dense balls along the stems, each flower about the size of a pinhead

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, rope-like stems that feel slightly fleshy and range from bright orange to pale yellow, often with a slightly waxy texture

idTips.label: Attachment Points
idTips.description: Small, knob-like structures called haustoria that penetrate the host plant's stem, appearing as tiny bumps where the dodder connects

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, round capsules that split open to release tiny seeds, usually developing after the small flower clusters fade

habitat: Hazel dodder is extremely rare in New England, preferring edges of woodlands and shrublands where it can find suitable host plants. It typically grows on hazel bushes, elderberry, and other native shrubs in partially sunny locations with good air circulation. Look for it in disturbed areas, woodland borders, and old field edges where shrubs are establishing.

seasonality.spring: Young dodder stems emerge and begin their search for host plants, appearing as thin orange threads reaching through the air.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when the orange vine masses are most visible, and tiny white flower clusters appear along the stems.
seasonality.fall: Stems may persist and continue growing until frost, with seed capsules developing and releasing seeds for next year.
seasonality.winter: The parasitic vines die back completely, leaving no trace above ground until seeds germinate the following spring.

funFact: Hazel dodder can actually 'smell' its preferred host plants and will grow toward them through the air, making looping motions until it detects the chemical scents of a suitable victim up to several inches away!
confusionNotes: With only one recorded observation in New England, hazel dodder is more likely to be confused with the much more common scaldweed dodder, which has similar orange thread-like stems. Hazel dodder specifically targets woody shrubs like hazel and elderberry, while scaldweed dodder prefers herbaceous plants in wetlands and field edges.
contextualKnowledge: Hazel dodder is so rare in New England that many botanists have never seen it in the wild here. It's much more common in the Midwest and western regions of North America, making any New England sighting quite noteworthy and worth documenting.
compareHints: Among New England's dodder species, hazel dodder is distinguished by its preference for woody shrubs rather than herbaceous plants. While scaldweed dodder tangles around grasses and wildflowers in wet areas, and field dodder prefers agricultural crops, hazel dodder specifically seeks out shrubs like hazel, elderberry, and similar woody hosts. Its orange stems tend to be slightly thicker and more robust than those of the more delicate herbaceous dodders.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Scaldweed differs from its dodder relatives primarily in where it grows - it prefers wetter habitats than Field Dodder, and its stems tend to be slightly thicker than Five Angled Dodder.
Compared to other dodders in New England, field dodder produces the largest seeds and tends to form denser, more tangled masses.

Buttonbush Dodder differs from other New England dodders primarily by its wetland habitat and host preferences - while Field Dodder attacks crops and Scaldweed Dodder prefers woodland edges, Buttonbush Dodder is the aquatic specialist of the family.
Lizard's tail dodder is distinguished from other New England dodders primarily by its wetland habitat and highly specific host preference for lizard's tail plants.
Sessile Dodder is unique among New England dodders for specializing on woody hosts rather than soft-stemmed plants.
Smartweed Dodder is distinguished from other New England dodders primarily by its habitat and host preferences - it's the wetland specialist of the dodder family.
Five Angled Dodder is much rarer in New England than the common Scaldweed dodder, and prefers wetter habitats compared to Field Dodder's preference for dry agricultural areas.
